title: The Unwritten Uniform
premise: In the waning years of a grinding continental war, Kestrel Dravenmoor serves as a battlefield nurse at Greyhollow Station, where he keeps a hidden ledger recording the names of soldiers that official reports omit — the uncounted dead. When a census taker named Elias Wren arrives asking one question too many about the station's missing men, Kestrel realizes the ledger could either condemn the officers who falsified records or finally give the forgotten their names back. As evacuation orders come and only one berth remains on the last transport out, Kestrel must choose between his ailing mentor Matron Sorrel, the orphaned ward Juniper who has become his found family, and Elias, whose investigation now makes him a target of the very command Kestrel's ledger indicts. In the end, Kestrel gives up his own berth, sends the ledger forward with Juniper, and stays behind with Elias to face the arriving tribunal — choosing love and truth over duty's arithmetic, and finding that what can be carried is not always what can be held.
about_author: Astrid Reyes is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime field hospitals before turning to fiction. She writes from a farmhouse library where she keeps her grandmother's nursing ledger open on the desk.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Cots
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A night of triage at Greyhollow Station establishes his ritual: after every shift he enters omitted names into a hidden ledger beneath the floorboards. The emotional beat is quiet grief disguised as bookkeeping, showing how he measures the world in what can be carried.

chapters.title: Names Not Entered
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. An officer orders three dead privates struck from the morning report; Kestrel copies their names into his ledger instead. Matron Sorrel catches him but says nothing, revealing she once kept such a ledger herself. Beat: complicity becomes inheritance.

chapters.title: The Census Taker's Question
chapters.summary: Elias Wren arrives to conduct the mandated census and asks why the station's headcount exceeds its recorded admissions. Kestrel deflects, but Elias notices the hesitation. Beat: first spark of wary fascination between two people counting the same war differently.

chapters.title: Juniper's Boots
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. The twelve-year-old ward who scrubs bandages narrates her day, revealing how the staff have become her family and how she idolizes Kestrel. She finds one loose floorboard and wisely says nothing. Beat: tenderness and the fragility of found family.

chapters.title: What the Orders Say
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. New commandant Colonel Vasseur institutes strict record discipline; discrepancies will be treated as treason. Kestrel must decide whether to bury the ledger or finish it. Beat: duty tightening like a tourniquet around conscience.

chapters.title: Rain on the Canvas Roof
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Stalled by weather, Elias works by lamplight and admits to himself the census is a pretext — his brother was one of the unrecorded dead. He suspects Greyhollow holds the answer. Beat: loneliness recognizing loneliness.

chapters.title: The Ledger Beneath
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Sorrel falls ill; before losing her voice to fever she tells Kestrel where her own wartime ledger lies and warns him that ledgers outlive their keepers. Beat: passing of the torch, dread braided with devotion.

chapters.title: An Inventory of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper trades contraband sugar for medicine for Sorrel, navigating the camp's black market. Kestrel covers for her theft. Beat: the family they've built committing small crimes to keep each other alive.

chapters.title: Two Ledgers, One Fire
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Vasseur burns a cache of 'irregular' files publicly as a warning. Kestrel watches pages curl, knowing his own could be next, and feels the ledger transform from habit to weapon. Beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias corners Kestrel with evidence of the falsified reports and asks directly about a private named Wren. Kestrel realizes Elias's brother may be in his ledger. Beat: collision of griefs; the blurb's pivotal moment lands.

chapters.title: Carry What You Can
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Evacuation orders arrive: the front is collapsing and Greyhollow will be abandoned. One berth remains on the last transport. Kestrel inventories everyone he loves against the space. Beat: the choice crystallizes, cold as arithmetic.

chapters.title: Sorrel's Hands
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper sits vigil with dying Sorrel, who mistakes her for a daughter lost long ago and calls her by name anyway. Beat: found family affirmed in the language of blood, heartbreak without bitterness.

chapters.title: Vasseur's Audit
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Vasseur announces a final audit before departure; every record will be reconciled or its keeper court-martialed. Elias is ordered off-station on the same transport. Beat: walls closing from every side at once.

chapters.title: What Elias Carried
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias confesses his true purpose to Kestrel and offers to destroy the ledger to save them all. Kestrel refuses: the names are the point. Beat: love declared not in words but in shared refusal.

chapters.title: The Berth
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel secretly lists Juniper for the last berth, forging Sorrel's authorization so no one can contest it. He tells no one, least of all Juniper. Beat: sacrifice made in silence, guilt already blooming.

chapters.title: Night of the Long Roll Call
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. The audit proceeds cot by cot while Kestrel hides the ledger inside Sorrel's belongings. Juniper discovers her name on the manifest and understands what it cost. Beat: terror, tenderness, and ticking clock converge.

chapters.title: Ashes Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Confronted by Vasseur, Kestrel chooses defiance: he reads the omitted names aloud before the assembled staff, making witnesses of them all. Beat: the climax — the ledger becomes testimony, and Kestrel becomes its voice.

chapters.title: The Last Transport
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper is loaded onto the transport clutching both ledgers, screaming Kestrel's name as the whistle blows. Elias steps off the train at the last second to stand beside him. Beat: devastating release; love chosen over survival.

chapters.title: Tribunal at Dawn
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel and Elias await arrest as Vasseur's superiors arrive — but the reading aloud worked: too many witnessed names for a quiet execution. An investigating magistrate demands the ledger. Beat: truth as shield, hope arriving sideways.

chapters.title: Reconciliation
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. The audit is redone honestly; Elias enters his brother's name into the official record with his own hand. Vasseur is relieved of command. Beat: justice as accounting, grief given a place in the count.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Sorrel dies at peace; Kestrel buries her beside the patients she never let go unnamed. He packs nothing but the clothes he wears and walks toward the rail line where Juniper's train went. Beat: mourning transmuted into direction.

chapters.title: The Unwritten Uniform
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV, months later. At a coastal town, Juniper waits at the station every evening with two ledgers. A figure in an unwritten uniform — no insignia, no rank — steps off the evening train: Kestrel, with Elias. Beat: reunion, inheritance fulfilled, the names finally home.
